In set theory, 
'''Cichoń's diagram'''  or '''Cichon's diagram''' is a table of 10 infinite [[cardinal number]]s related to the [[set theory of the reals]] displaying the provable relations between these 
[[Cardinal characteristic of the continuum|cardinal characteristics of the continuum]].  All these cardinals are greater than or equal to <math>\aleph_1</math>, the smallest uncountable cardinal, and they are bounded above by <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>, the [[cardinality of the continuum]].  Four cardinals describe properties of the [[ideal on a set|ideal]] of sets of [[Lebesgue measure|measure zero]]; four more describe the corresponding properties of the ideal of [[meagre set|meager sets (first category sets)]].

==Definitions==

Let ''I'' be a proper [[ideal on a set|ideal]] of a fixed infinite set ''X'', containing all finite subsets of ''X''. We define the following "[[Cardinal function|cardinal coefficients]]" of ''I'':

*<math>\operatorname{add}(I)=\min\{|{\mathcal A}|: {\mathcal A}\subseteq I \wedge \bigcup{\mathcal A}\notin I\big\}.</math>
::The "additivity" of ''I'' is the smallest number of sets from ''I'' whose union is not in ''I''.   As any ideal is closed under finite unions, this number is always at least <math>\aleph_0</math>; if ''I'' is a &sigma;-ideal, then add(''I'')&nbsp;&ge;&nbsp;<math>\aleph_1</math>.
*<math>\operatorname{cov}(I)=\min\{|{\mathcal A}|:{\mathcal A}\subseteq I \wedge\bigcup{\mathcal A} = X\big\}.</math>
:: The "covering number" of ''I'' is the smallest number of sets from ''I'' whose union is all of ''X''.  As ''X'' itself is not in ''I'', we must have add(''I'') &le; cov(''I'').
*<math>\operatorname{non}(I)=\min\{|\mathcal{A}|:\mathcal{A}\subseteq X\ \wedge\ \mathcal{A}\notin I\big\},</math>
:: The "uniformity number" of ''I'' (sometimes also written <math>\operatorname{unif}(I)</math>) is the size of the smallest set not in ''I''.  By our assumption on ''I'', add(''I'') &le; non(''I'').
*<math>\operatorname{cof}(I)=\min\{|{\mathcal A}|:{\mathcal A}\subseteq I \wedge (\forall B\in I)(\exists A\in {\mathcal A})(B\subseteq A)\big\}.</math>
:: The "cofinality" of ''I'' is the [[cofinality]] of the [[partial order]] (''I'', &sube;). It is easy to see that we must have non(''I'') &le; cof(''I'') and cov(''I'') &le; cof(''I'').

Furthermore, the "[[bounding number]]" or "unboundedness number" <math>{\mathfrak b}</math> and the "[[dominating number]]" <math>{\mathfrak d}</math> are defined as follows:
*<math>{\mathfrak b}=\min\big\{|F|:F\subseteq{\mathbb N}^{\mathbb N}\ \wedge\ (\forall g\in {\mathbb N}^{\mathbb N})(\exists f\in F)(\exists^\infty n\in{\mathbb N})(g(n)<f(n))\big\},</math>
*<math>{\mathfrak d}=\min\big\{|F|:F\subseteq{\mathbb N}^{\mathbb N}\ \wedge\ (\forall g\in{\mathbb N}^{\mathbb N})(\exists f\in F)(\forall^\infty n\in{\mathbb N})(g(n)<f(n))\big\},</math>
where  "<math>\exists^\infty n\in{\mathbb N}</math>" means: "there are infinitely many natural numbers ''n'' such that&nbsp;…", and "<math>\forall^\infty n\in{\mathbb N}</math>" means "for all except finitely many natural numbers ''n'' we have&nbsp;…".

==Diagram==
Let <math>{\mathcal B}</math> be the  σ-ideal of those subsets of the real line that are [[meager set|meager]] (or "of the first category") in the [[euclidean topology]], and let 
<math>{\mathcal L}</math> be the σ-ideal of those subsets of the real line that are of [[Lebesgue measure]] zero. Then the following inequalities hold:

{| style="text-align: center; margin: 1em auto;"  |
|-
| || ||  <math>\operatorname{cov}(\mathcal L)</math> || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
|        <math>\operatorname{non}(\mathcal B)</math> || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
|        <math>\operatorname{cof}(\mathcal B)</math> || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
|        <math>\operatorname{cof}(\mathcal L)</math> || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
| <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>
|- align=center |
| ||
| || || <math>\uparrow</math>    ||
| <math>\uparrow</math>    ||
|- align=center |
| || 
| <math>\Bigg\uparrow</math> ||
| <math>\mathfrak b</math>  || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
| <math>\mathfrak d</math> ||
| <math>\Bigg\uparrow</math>
|- align=center |
|  || ||
| ||  <math>\uparrow</math>    ||
| <math>\uparrow</math>
|-
|<math>\aleph_1</math>                || <math>\longrightarrow</math>
|<math>\operatorname{add}{(\mathcal L)}</math> ||<math>\longrightarrow</math>
|<math>\operatorname{add}{(\mathcal B)}</math> ||<math>\longrightarrow</math>
|<math>\operatorname{cov}{(\mathcal B)}</math> ||<math>\longrightarrow</math>
|<math>\operatorname{non}{(\mathcal L)}</math>
|}

Where an arrow from <math>x</math> to <math>y</math> is to mean that <math>x\le y</math>. In addition, the following relations  hold: 
{{center|
<math>\operatorname{add}({\mathcal B})=\min\{\operatorname{cov}({\mathcal B}),{\mathfrak b}\}</math>  and 
<math>\operatorname{cof}({\mathcal B})=\max\{\operatorname{non}({\mathcal B}),{\mathfrak d}\}.</math><ref name="survey">
{{citation
| last = Bartoszyński | first = Tomek | authorlink = Tomek Bartoszyński
| year = 2009
| contribution = Invariants of Measure and Category
| editor-last = Foreman |editor-first=Matthew
| title = Handbook of Set Theory
| pages = 491–555
| publisher = Springer-Verlag
| arxiv = math/9910015
| doi = 10.1007/978-1-4020-5764-9_8
| isbn = 978-1-4020-4843-2
| s2cid = 15079978 }}</ref>}}

It turns out that the inequalities described by the diagram, together with the relations mentioned above, are all the relations between these cardinals that are provable in [[ZFC]], in the following limited sense. Let ''A'' be any assignment of the cardinals <math>\aleph_1</math> and <math>\aleph_2</math> to the 10 cardinals in Cichoń's diagram. Then if ''A'' is consistent with the diagram's relations, and if ''A'' also satisfies the two additional relations, then ''A'' can be realized in some [[model (model theory)|model]] of ZFC.

For larger continuum sizes, the situation is less clear.  It is consistent with ZFC that all of the Cichoń's diagram cardinals are simultaneously different apart from <math>\operatorname{add}({\mathcal B})</math> and <math>\operatorname{cof}({\mathcal B})</math>  (which are equal to other entries).<ref>{{citation
| author1 = [[Martin Goldstern]] | author2 = Jakob Kellner | author3 = [[Saharon Shelah]]
| year = 2019
| title = Cichoń's maximum
| arxiv = 1708.03691
| journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]]
| volume = 190
| number = 1
| pages = 113–143
| doi = 10.4007/annals.2019.190.1.2
| s2cid = 119654292
}}</ref><ref>{{citation
| author1 = Martin Goldstern | author2 = Jakob Kellner | author3 = Diego A. Mejía | author4 = Saharon Shelah
| year = 2019
| title = Cichoń's maximum without large cardinals
| arxiv = 1906.06608
}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|author1=Martin Goldstern |author2=Jakob Kellner|title=A Deep Math Dive into Why Some Infinities Are Bigger Than Others |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/a-deep-math-dive-into-why-some-infinities-are-bigger-than-others/ |access-date=2021-08-23|website=Scientific American}}</ref>

Some inequalities in the diagram (such as "add &le; cov") follow immediately from the definitions. The inequalities <math>\operatorname{cov}({\mathcal B}) \le \operatorname{non}({\mathcal L})</math> and 
<math>\operatorname{cov}({\mathcal L}) \le \operatorname{non}({\mathcal B})</math> are classical theorems 
<!-- Sierpinski?? -->and follow from the fact that the real line can be partitioned into a meager set and a set of measure zero.

==Remarks==

The British mathematician [[David Fremlin]] named the diagram after  the Polish mathematician from [[Wrocław]], {{ill|Jacek Cichoń|pl}}.<ref>{{citation|last=Fremlin|first=David H.|contribution=Cichon's diagram|series=Publ. Math. [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]]|volume=66|title=Sémin. Initiation Anal. 23ème Année-1983/84|id=Exp. No.5, 13 p.|year=1984|zbl=0559.03029}}.</ref>

The [[continuum hypothesis]], of <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math> being equal to <math>\aleph_1</math>, would make all of these relations equalities.

[[Martin's axiom]], a weakening of the continuum hypothesis, implies that all cardinals in the diagram (except perhaps <math>\aleph_1</math>) are equal to <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>.

Similar diagrams can be drawn for cardinal characteristics of higher cardinals <math>\kappa</math> for <math>\kappa</math> [[Inaccessible cardinal|strongly inaccessible]], which assort various cardinals between <math>\kappa^+</math> and <math>2^\kappa</math>.<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=1806.08583 |doi=10.4064/fm666-4-2020 |title=The higher Cichoń diagram |date=2021 |last1=Shelah |first1=Saharon |last2=Goldstern |first2=Martin |last3=Baumhauer |first3=Thomas |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |volume=252 |issue=3 |pages=241–314 |s2cid=111385070 }}</ref>
